gov.c1.p: A contract between web UIs and the agents that drive them. Apache-2.0, edited here, changed through a public RFC process.
gov.c2.p: A way of building software with AI in which the owner verifies evidence instead of reading code. Different author, Creative Commons BY-SA 4.0, and it works without us.
gov.c3.p: Commercial software that implements the method and speaks the protocol. Useful, optional, and not to be confused with either.
gov.h2: Three different things, three different licences.
gov.why.label: Why we say it this way
gov.why.p: Because readers — and the AI assistants they ask — keep collapsing the three into one product narrative. A protocol you can implement without us, a method you can follow with any tool, and a product we sell are not the same kind of thing, and conflating them is the fastest way to misjudge all three.
hero.h1: Stable names for the things an agent wants to act on.
hero.lede: NAC3 is a small, free contract that lets a web UI you already shipped be driven by AI assistants, voice runners, RPA bots, accessibility tools and test runners — by name, not by brittle selectors. You add a few HTML attributes. Agents resolve names, click buttons, fill fields and switch tabs the way a person would, and the contract itself is published as data, with a hash you recompute.
hero.t4: · Immutable runtime path, verified by hash
limits.h2: NAC3 names what lives in the DOM. Everything here is outside that line.
limits.l1.p: NAC3 does not read pixels. In a document editor or a design tool the toolbar around the drawing can be named; the drawing cannot. A plugin can declare how its verbs route to the app's own API — somebody still has to write it.
limits.l2.p: A component mounted closed is unreachable unless its author exposes a resolver. That is a browser security boundary, not our decision, and the runtime reports it instead of guessing. Open roots are covered, nested.
limits.l3.p: An embedded page from another origin cannot be driven unless it cooperates. When it does not, the runtime fails closed rather than pretending the click landed.
limits.l4.h: Anything that is not the web
limits.l4.p: NAC3 is HTML attributes. Desktop, mobile-native and terminal applications are out of scope.
limits.l5.h: It is not a permission system
limits.l5.p: A named verb is an intent-level signal and the capability gate is a usability optimisation. Your server must still authorise every call.
limits.l6.h: A declared schema is not a validated one
limits.l6.p: A manifest may carry a payload schema and the reference runtime never reads it. An agent must not assume a payload was checked.
limits.l7.p: Stable names are a promise you keep, not one we enforce. Rename an id and every caller that used it breaks, the same way a changed URL breaks a bookmark.
limits.l8.h: It does not make an agent correct
limits.l8.p: In our own 600-run benchmark NAC3 reached 95.5%, not 100%. What it removes is silent damage — 0 of 200 runs against 30 of 200 on raw DOM — not the need to check what an agent did.
limits.lede: We would rather you read this before you migrate than discover it after.
limits.lic.urazuke: Urazuke, the method — Creative Commons BY-SA 4.0
limits.steward: One more limit lives in its own section, because it is about who steers the contract rather than what it reaches: NAC3 is stewarded by one company, not a foundation.
limits.three.label: Three different things, three different licences
limits.three.p: NAC3 is a protocol, Urazuke is a method for building software with evidence, and Forge is a commercial tool that implements both. You can adopt the protocol without the method and without the tool — that is what publishing it under Apache-2.0 is for.

pay.f.p: The specification, the reference runtime, the published contract API, the validator, the CLI, every guide and all nine demos. Apache-2.0: use it, fork it, implement it, ship it commercially. No permission needed and nothing to pay.
pay.h2: The contract is free. The tooling on top of it is not.
pay.lede: This distinction matters more than it looks, so here it is in one place. Nothing on the paid side is required to implement, adopt, test or ship NAC3.
pay.p.byok: Both are bring-your-own-key: the subscription covers the tooling, never the AI consumption. You pay your model provider directly.
pay.p.l1: Forge — USD 10/month, in alpha. A voice-first development framework whose output is compliant on day one, with generated end-to-end tests.
pay.p.l2: Pilot — USD 5/month, free with Forge, shipping next. One controller — voice, chat, keyboard — across every compliant app in the registry.
pay.p.p: Two products built on the contract, by the same team that edits it. They make adoption faster. They are not the contract, and the contract does not need them.
review.b1: The specification mandates ten locales for your labels and has a single normative language. Defensible — English is the working language of the trade — and now said out loud instead of left as an apparent inconsistency: the English text governs, and the nine translations published beside it declare themselves non-normative, with the revision they came from and how much of the current text they carry. What is still open is that none of them is complete.
review.b2: Adoption rests on a promise nothing enforces. Stable ids are the whole value, and the project correctly says it has no way to make you keep them. That is honest, and it is the single biggest risk to anyone building on it: rename an id and every caller breaks, exactly as a changed URL breaks a bookmark.
review.b3: A declared payload schema is not a validated one. A manifest may carry one and the reference runtime never reads it. The spec says so. It still means a conformant host can advertise a shape it does not check.
review.b4: Stewardship is one vendor. The RFC process and the governance page are real, but the editor, the reference runtime and the flagship adopter are the same organisation. Normal at this stage, and the thing a second independent implementer would change.
review.c1: The specification end to end: roles, names, verbs, the manifest, the public API, the event family, provenance, the three conformance levels, versioning and the stability guarantees.
review.c2: The published contract as data — the directory, the version pointers, and the per-version contract, finding catalogue and conformance levels — fetched from the live site and read the way a consumer would.
review.c3: The runtime bytes served from the immutable path, and the integrity hash in the install snippet above.
review.c4: The deploy chain: every push to the default branch passes an integrity gate, a version-coherence gate, a validator lock and a contract-API gate — each with its own deliberate-red test — and then smoke-checks the live site from outside.
review.c5: Every demo and document this page links, including the compiled React and Angular study cases.
review.g1: Failing closed on ambiguity. Two reservations sharing a suffix used to resolve to whichever matched first. Since v2.4 that throws, names the candidates and emits an event so the host can ask “did you mean A or B?”. An agent protocol that guesses quietly is worse than no protocol, because the damage is invisible. This one stopped guessing on purpose, and published the migration.
review.g2: The contract is data, not prose. Roles, verbs, events, finding codes and conformance levels are fetchable as JSON, versioned, with a hash a consumer recomputes. Most specifications in this space ask you to parse a markdown file or read their implementation. This one does not.
review.g3: It tells you when not to use it. The comparison table says plainly that if you are inside one app with one agent vendor, MCP plus a good ARIA pass covers most of it. A project that names the case against itself is a project you can plan around.
review.g4: Every figure carries a receipt. Run date, runtime version, raw output, the command to re-run, and an explicit note when a number has not been re-measured on a later release. Cheap to write, rare to find, and the only reason the measurements below are worth reading.
review.g5: The integrity story is complete. Immutable path, subresource hash, a gate that refuses to deploy a stale hash, and a smoke check that the live page still serves it. That chain did not exist five months ago.
review.h2: A review by a model that read the whole thing.
review.lede: This page used to carry one-line verdicts from six AI systems, collected in May 2026. They were enthusiastic and they were not useful: none of them had read the runtime, none had verified a single claim, and “architecturally inevitable” is not a finding. We took them down. What follows is one review instead of six, by a model given access to the source, the published contract, the deploy chain and the live site, and that says what it checked.
review.quote: “The valuable idea here is not that an agent can click a button. It is that NAC3 turns an unbounded perception problem into a bounded naming problem — and then refuses to guess when the name is ambiguous. That second half is the engineering, and it is the half most of this category skips.”
review.receipt.label: Receipt
review.receipt.p1: This is the opinion of a language model. It is not a measurement and not an audit certificate. What it rests on is listed above and can be repeated: the specification, the contract API, the runtime bytes, the deploy workflow and the live endpoints are all public.
review.receipt.p2: The same reviewer audited this project earlier in 2026, and several items listed above as strengths — the integrity chain, the contract as data, the limits section, the receipts — were opened as defects then and closed since. That is a conflict of interest worth knowing about, and it is why the weaknesses are listed with the same specificity as the strengths.
review.verdict: Worth adopting if you have more than one caller — voice and chat and tests and RPA — or workflows that cross apps, or you want integrations that survive a change of agent vendor. Not worth the mental cost if you only need stable selectors for a test suite: use data-testid and come back when the second caller arrives. And read the limits section before you migrate, not after.
review.who: — Claude (Opus 5), 26 October 2026, at the maintainer's request.
stack.h2: NAC3 is the client-side half. MCP is the server-side half.
stack.honest.label: Honest read
stack.honest.p: If you are inside a single app with a single agent vendor, MCP on the server plus a screen-reader-grade ARIA pass on the client covers most cases. NAC3 starts paying back when you have multiple callers, cross-app workflows, or you want integrations that outlive your choice of agent vendor.
stack.lede: It does not compete with the tools below: it overlaps narrowly and complements in others. If you have one of these problems, use the dedicated tool. If you have several, the contract unifies them.
stack.r1a: The agent calls server-side tools and functions.
stack.r1b: Does not touch the UI: the agent cannot navigate, fill a form or read on-screen state.
stack.r1c: Complement. MCP for backend operations, NAC3 for the UI half.
stack.r2a: An accessibility tree for screen readers and switch devices.
stack.r2b: Stops at “this is a button named Save”: no verb to call, no completion event.
stack.r2c: Sits next to. Keep your roles. Many adopters carry both attributes on the same element.
stack.r3b: Test-only: no manifest, no event family, no provenance, no i18n.
stack.r3c: Superset, at a higher mental cost. If you only need tests, data-testid is fine.
stack.r4a: An agent-to-app protocol for chat-driven UIs.
stack.r4b: Tied to its framework and runtime; less focus on RPA, accessibility and cross-vendor models.
stack.r4c: Adjacent. A different bet on the same space, funded and with an ecosystem. Pick it if you build on that framework.
stack.r5a: The agent reads pixels and reasons over screenshots.
stack.r5b: Slow, expensive, brittle on dynamic content, and entirely dependent on the model.
stack.r5c: Fallback layer. Vision is what the agent uses when the contract is absent.
tr.h2: The English text governs. Nine machine translations stand beside it.
tr.lede: The normative text of NAC3 is the English specification. The nine translations below are non-normative machine translations: none of them is complete, and where a translation and the English text disagree the English text governs — a conformance claim is a claim against the English text. Each page states at the top, in its own language, which revision it was translated from and how much of the current text it carries.
tr.note: A partial translation a reader can check against the English text is worth more than no translation — as long as the page says which one governs before the reader starts trusting it. Bringing them up to the current text is open work, not a silent gap. And the ten-locale requirement of the specification is a requirement on the labels in your manifest, not on the language of this document.
tr.note.label: Why we publish them anyway
ura.caveat: Said plainly: you do not need NAC3 to apply Urazuke, and you do not need Urazuke to use NAC3. They are a method and a protocol, by different authors, under different licences. They meet at exactly one point — step zero's testability criterion — and that point is where using both costs less than using either alone.
ura.h2: 裏付け  If you build with the Urazuke method, this is where NAC3 pays for itself.
ura.l1: The method asks for the capability, not for us. Urazuke states explicitly that NAC3 is not a requirement — it is one way its author reaches that capability today. Any technology whose interface exposes its elements to a driver satisfies the gate.
ura.l2: What NAC3 adds is that the names survive. A test says NAC.click('invoice.save'). The design team moves that button from a toolbar into a dropdown. The test keeps passing. That is the difference between a suite you maintain and a suite you rewrite.
ura.l3: And the suite can be generated. From a manifest: one test per role and acknowledgement family, across Playwright, Cypress, Vitest and WebdriverIO. In the case study below that produced 66 end-to-end tests — 4.7× more cases than the fork's hand-written suite.
ura.lede: Urazuke is a free method for building software with AI in which the owner of the project verifies evidence instead of reading code. Its very first gate — step zero — excludes any technology that cannot be tested end to end: you have to be able to drive the screen by program, click, type and read state, and then verify that the change actually reached the backend. If you cannot, somebody ends up reading code, which is the one thing the method promises to avoid.
uses.h2: Voice and chat is the headline. The contract underneath unlocks four more.
uses.u1.p: Voice runners and chat agents drive the same UI a person uses, by stable name, in ten locales out of the box.
uses.u2.p: Switch devices, head-trackers, eye-gaze, braille displays and predictive keyboards get a stable target tree without a per-app retrofit. Where ARIA stops at “this is a button”, NAC3 says “this button has a verb you can call”.
uses.u3.p: Names that survive redesigns, consumed by Selenium, Playwright, Cypress and headless browsers alike. Test corpora can be generated per role and acknowledgement family.
uses.u4.p: No brittle CSS, no screenshot OCR, no XPath rituals: the bot reads the description, picks an action by verb and waits on the canonical event. One bot drives ten vendors' apps if all ten implement the contract.
uses.u5.p: Models drive web UIs by name with no per-app fine-tuning, and a host agent can import a peer app's tree and proxy dispatches into it.
what.h2: A button you already shipped, with three extra attributes.
what.lede: That is the whole adoption cost of one element. No framework to adopt, no build step to add, no runtime to rewrite your app around.
what.runtime.h: Add the runtime once — and pin it
what.runtime.p: Production pins the immutable path and lets the browser verify the bytes. js/2.5.2/nac.js never changes; js/nac.js is a moving alias for trying things, never for pinning.
